query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An advanced free‐energy sampling method augmented by machine‐learning interatomic potentials can accurately and efficiently predict the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase free energies of high‐entropy alloys, yielding results within a narrow error margin compared to experimental calorimetric data across a broad range of HEA compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-state high-entropy alloys (HEAs), particularly refractory BCC-phase systems such as NbMoTaW-related compositions.
generation.intervention: Implementation of an enhanced sampling molecular dynamics simulation framework using thermodynamic integration and machine-learning interatomic potentials calibrated at high temperatures.
generation.conditions: High-temperature near melting under equilibrium or near-equilibrium conditions, applied across compositional variants within the HEA family.
generation.structural_mediator: A simulation framework that explicitly resolves configurational entropy, interfacial energies, and bulk free energies during the solid-to-liquid transition.
generation.mechanism: The method integrates advanced free-energy sampling with machine-learned potentials to capture detailed energetic contributions from all constituent elements, overcoming limitations of averaging techniques and traditional calorimetric methods.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulated melting properties (i.e., melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase free energies) that agree within approximately 5-10% of benchmark experimental measurements, demonstrating improved accuracy and efficiency versus conventional approaches.
generation.baseline: Conventional calorimetric experiments and averaged computational models, which often provide insufficient resolution for the complex phase behavior in multi-component HEAs.
generation.boundary: Applicability is expected to be robust for HEAs exhibiting refractory behavior and single-phase BCC structures, but it may be limited for compositions with significant multiphase or non-equilibrium solidification behavior.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative performance metrics and error margins remain uncertain pending full calibration of the machine-learning potentials; further, the approach’s scalability across all HEA compositional spaces is not yet fully validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of benchmark HEA compositions with well-characterized melting properties via independent calorimetric measurements. Perform simulations using the advanced free-energy sampling method with calibrated machine-learning interatomic potentials. Compare the predicted melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change, and liquid-phase free energies against experimental data.
measurements: Volume change at melting (% or cm3/mol)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any predicted thermodynamic parameter deviates by more than about 10% from the experimental benchmark under defined high-temperature equilibrium conditions, the effectiveness of the proposed approach will be ruled out.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

“Superalloy” is the general name given to iron-based, nickel-based, and cobalt-based alloys, given their high endurance, creep, and fatigue strength at high temperature. They are widely used in aviation, aerospace, and automotive and chemical industries, serving in high-temperature (≤ 1100 °C) environments. However, for super high temperature conditions of up to 1500 °C and 3000 °C, traditional surperalloys are powerless. Instead, a new type of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown their advantages. High-entropy alloys or multi-element alloys are loosely defined as solid-solution alloys that contain more than five principal elements in equal or near equal atomic percent (at%) [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. HEAs usually have unexpected properties, such as high strength, high hardness, excellent softening resistance, and wear and corrosion resistance [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. According to the cocktail effects of HEAs, the alloy properties can be adjusted by composition changes and via alloying [ [4] , [5] , [10] ]. Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. For comparison, a counterpart alloy with the same chemical composition was analyzed and produced by an AMF process. The microstructures of the tested alloys were examined by scanning electron micro

This basic feasibility analysis addresses the question of whether HEA WTaMoNbV can be adequately produced via the LPBF process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. In fact, the more fundamental question is whether the proposed LPBF process is capable of adequately synthesizing the alloying elements of HEA [ [12] ] in a similar manner to that obtained using a conventional AMF process [ [36] ].

The attained results clearly demonstrated that the macrostructure and phase composition of samples produced by LPBF were similar to those obtained by its counterpart AMF alloy. In both cases, the alloys were composed of a single solid-phase solution with a BCC crystal structure with similar lattice parameters, as expected according to Kang et al. [ [48] ]. In terms of microstructure, both alloys showed differences in the distribution of tungsten and an increased amount of vanadium at grain boundaries. This can mainly be related to the relatively low melting temperature of vanadium (1910 °C) versus tungsten (3422 °C), which consequently causes vanadium to solidify at grain boundaries during the final phase of the solidification process. decision.trend: Early HEA studies primarily focused on processing routes and the resulting mechanical and microstructural properties – for example, SLM- and LPBF-based investigations (PMC6427779 and PMC9229239) have advanced our control over high-temperature melting and solidification in complex alloys. Alongside experimental techniques (such as traditional calorimetry) and standard computational thermodynamic models, researchers have gradually shifted toward high-throughput and machine‐learning–assisted strategies. However, while these approaches successfully capture many aspects of phase formation and mechanical behavior near melting, they stop short of directly and comprehensively determining thermodynamic fusion parameters such as melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and liquid-phase free energies. Thus, the field demonstrates a historical progression from conventional, often under-resolved measurement techniques toward more sophisticated, simulation-driven methods – yet the specific challenge of reliable, broad-range thermodynamic characterization of melting in HEAs remains open.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved problem is to develop a method that can accurately and efficiently quantify melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the vast compositional space of high‐entropy alloys. Current experimental and computational approaches encounter limitations in precision and scalability owing to the compositional complexity and non-ideal phase behaviors. Moreover, a decisive validation or falsification criterion (i.e. a clear experimental benchmark that the method must meet) has not been established to ensure the reliability of any new approach.
decision.lever: Develop and deploy an advanced free-energy sampling method (e.g., thermodynamic integration or enhanced sampling MD) augmented by machine-learning interatomic potentials calibrated against high-temperature benchmarks. Key parameters would include rigorous treatment of configurational entropy, accurate estimation of interfacial and bulk free energies, and systematic error quantification.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of moving from conventional calorimetric and averaged computational methods – which struggle with the inherent complexity of HEAs – to more sophisticated, simulation-based techniques. Enhanced free-energy sampling directly addresses the challenge by focusing on the detailed energetics of phase transformation during melting. By linking simulation outputs to decisive experimental validations (e.g., matching calorimetric measurements within a narrow error margin across diverse compositions), this method provides a physically grounded, efficient, and generalizable solution that can falsify a candidate model if key fusion parameters do not align with measured values.
